newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian rescuers seek survivors of "terrorist act".
newsitem.headline: Russian rescuers seek survivors of "terrorist act".

text.p: Rescue workers on Sunday frantically sifted through the ruins of a military block of flats for survivors of an explosion that border guards said was an attempt by gangsters to scare the authorities.
The death toll from the blast, which happened early on Saturday in Russia's southern Dagestan region, had reached 24, including nine children, by Sunday evening, officials said.
Tass said a third of the Caspian region's border guards might have been wiped out in the explosion.
A spokesman for Dagestani authorities said 24 dead and eight injured people had been pulled from the ruins of the eight- storey building and 35 were still assumed to be in the rubble.
Tass quoted official sources as saying it might be a gangland revenge attack linked to a regional crackdown on arms and caviar smuggling.
The border guards issued a statement describing the explosion as a "terrorist act" by cross-border criminals.
"Those who thus intend to intimidate the border defenders are deeply mistaken," it said, adding that the losses had strengthened their resolve to deal harshly with the criminals.
It called on the relevant state institutions to deal with the "outrageous outburst of crime and terrorism" in the country.

Gangland violence has become commonplace in post-communist Russia. Last weekend 14 people died in a bomb blast at a Moscow cemetery apparently triggered by a feud between warring factions of an Afghan war veterans' charity with big business links.
Rescue workers planned to work through a second night digging for survivors.
"We expect to get into the basement of the building tonight, which will shed some light on the cause of the blast," said a spokesman for the local emergencies ministry department.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin flew to this small port by the Caspian Sea on Sunday after promising a thorough investigation into the disaster.
The blast occurred while residents, mostly families of border guards and airforce officers, were sleeping.
"I thought I was having a bad dream. Everything began falling on me and then a man called Akhmed rescued me," 12-year-old Roxana told Reuters at a local hospital where many of the injured were taken.
Rescue workers, including teams flown in from Moscow, used cranes, sniffer dogs and electric drills to hunt for survivors.

By Sunday afternoon they were dragging out mostly dead bodies but Russian public television said the rescuers had found a man alive on Sunday evening after briefly silencing their equipment in the hope of hearing cries for help from survivors.
Regional authorities have declared Sunday and Monday official days of mourning in Dagestan, which borders the breakaway Russian republic of Chechnya.
Some officials said there might be a link between the explosion and Chechnya, where an uneasy peace is holding after a 21-month bloody conflict between Russian forces and separatists.
Local residents shared that suspicions.
"Those bloody Chechens are responsible for this," one woman told Chernomyrdin as he toured the scene of the disaster.

But Chechen rebel leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, whose aide worked out a new draft agreement with Moscow on Saturday, on Sunday denied the separatists were involved in the blast, which he said was aimed at wrecking the peace process.

The border guards said the blast could not have been caused by a gas leak because the building was not connected to gas mains. Agencies reported signs that TNT explosive had been detonated in the building.

President Boris Yeltsin, recovering from heart surgery, has sent his condolences to relatives of the dead and the government has set up a commission under a deputy prime minister, Oleg Lobov, to investigate the causes of the blast.
